source_text: Quaesisti proxime, Fabi frater, fugiendum necne sit in persecutione, quod nescio quid annuntiaretur. Ibidem ego oblocutus aliquid pro loco ac tempore et quarundam personarum importunitate semitractatam materiam abstuli mecum plenius eam de stilo nunc renuntiaturus, utpote quam mihi tua consultatio commendarat et condicio temporum suo iam nomine iniunxerat. Quanto enim frequentiores imminent persecutiones, tanto examinatio procuranda est, quomodo eas excipere fides debeat. Procuranda autem examinatio penes vos, qui, si forte, paracletum non recipiendo deductorem omnis veritatis merito adhuc etiam aliis quaestionibus obnixi estis. Igitur consultationi tuae ordinem quoque induimus, animadvertentes ante determinari oportere de statu ipsius persecutionis, utrum a deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu eius constare possit. Omnis enim rei inspectio auctore cognito planior. Satis est quidem praescribere nihil fieri sine dei voluntate. Sed non statim hac sententia ceteris retractatibus locum dabimus, ne a praesenti articulo avocemur, si qui responderit: Ergo et malum a deo et delictum a deo, nihil iam in diabolo, nihil etiam in nobis ipsis. De persecutione nunc quaeritur. Circa hanc interim dixerim nihil fieri sine dei voluntate, respiciens eam inprimis dignam deo esse et, ut ita dixerim, necessariam, ad probationem scilicet servorum eius sive reprobationem. Quis est enim exitus persecutionis, quis effectus alius, nisi probatio et reprobatio fidei, qua suos utique dominus examinabit? Hoc domini iudicium est persecutio, per quam quis aut probatus aut reprobatus iudicatur. Porro iudicium soli deo competit. Haec pala illa, quae et nunc dominicam aream purgat, ecclesiam scilicet, confusum acervum fidelium eventilans et discernens frumentum martyrum et paleas negatorum, et haec etiam scalae, quas somniat Iacob, aliis ascensum in superiora, aliis descensum ad inferiora demonstrantes. Sic et agonem intellegi capit persecutionem. A quo certamen edicitur, nisi a quo corona et praemia proponuntur? Legis edictum agonis istius in Apocalypsi, quibus praemiis ad victoriam invitet vel maxime illos qui proprie vicerint in persecutione, vincendo luctati revera non adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed adversus spiritalia nequitiae. Ita agnosces ad eundem agonothetam pertinere certaminis arbitrium qui invitat ad praemium. Totum quod agitur in persecutione gloria dei est, probantis et reprobantis, imponentis et deponentis. Quod autem ad gloriam dei pertinet, utique ex voluntate illius eveniet. Sed quando deus magis creditur, nisi cum magis timetur? nisi in tempore persecutionis? Ecclesia in attonito est. Tunc et fides in expeditione sollicitior et disciplinatior in ieiuniis et stationibus et orationibus et humilitate, in alterutra diligentia et dilectione, in sanctitate et sobrietate. Non enim vacatur nisi timori et spei. Adeo et ex hoc ipso ostenditur nobis non posse diabolo deputari eam quae meliores efficit dei servos.
thought_title: Persecution is God's testing, not the devil's work
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by answering Fabius's question whether one should flee in persecution, and begins by establishing that persecution comes from God for the testing of faith.
pass_a_gloss: You asked recently, brother Fabius, whether one must flee or not in persecution, because something or other was being announced. On that occasion I spoke something in reply, as place and time allowed and because of the importunity of certain persons, and I took away with me the half-treated subject, intending now to report it more fully from the pen, since your consultation had entrusted it to me and the condition of the times had already by its own name imposed it. For the more frequent the persecutions that threaten, the more an examination must be provided, how faith ought to receive them. But the examination must be provided among you, who, if perhaps, by not receiving the Comforter, the guide of all truth, are deservedly still also entangled in other questions. Therefore I have also imposed an order on your consultation, observing that it must first be determined about the status of persecution itself, whether it comes from God or from the devil, so that more easily it can be established about its outcome. For the inspection of every thing is plainer when its author is known. It is enough indeed to prescribe that nothing happens without the will of God. But I will not immediately by this sentence give room to other retractations, lest we be called away from the present point, if someone should answer: Therefore both evil is from God and sin is from God, nothing now is in the devil, nothing even in ourselves. About persecution the question is now. Around this for the present I would say that nothing happens without the will of God, considering it in the first place worthy of God and, so to speak, necessary, namely for the testing of his servants or their rejection. For what is the outcome of persecution, what other effect, except the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord will certainly examine his own? This judgment of the Lord is persecution, through which each person is judged either tested or rejected. Moreover judgment belongs to God alone. This is that winnowing fan, which even now cleanses the Lord's threshing floor, namely the church, winnowing the confused heap of believers and separating the grain of martyrs and the chaff of deniers, and these are also the ladders, which Jacob dreams, showing to some an ascent to higher things, to others a descent to lower things. So also persecution can be understood as a contest. By whom is the contest proclaimed, except by whom the crown and rewards are offered? You read the edict of this contest in Revelation, with what rewards he invites to victory especially those who have properly conquered in persecution, by conquering having wrestled truly not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness. So you will recognize that to the same contest-president belongs the arbitration of the contest who invites to the reward. Everything that is done in persecution is the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who raises up and casts down. But what pertains to the glory of God will certainly come about from his will. But when is God more believed, except when he is more feared? except in the time of persecution? The church is in astonishment. Then also faith is more anxious in its expedition and more disciplined in fasts and stations and prayers and humility, in mutual diligence and love, in holiness and sobriety. For there is no leisure except for fear and hope. So also from this very thing it is shown to us that it cannot be assigned to the devil, that which makes better the servants of God.

pass_b_english: You asked me recently, brother Fabius, whether one should flee in persecution or not, because something was being announced, though I do not know what. I answered on the spot, as the place and time allowed and as the insistence of certain people demanded, and I carried away with me the subject only half treated. Now I intend to set it out more fully in writing, since your consultation entrusted it to me and the condition of the times had already laid it upon me by its very name. For the more frequent the persecutions that threaten, the more carefully we must examine how faith ought to receive them. And this examination must be undertaken among you, who by not receiving the Comforter, the guide into all truth, are deservedly still struggling with other questions as well.

So I have given your consultation an ordered structure, observing that the first thing to be determined is the status of persecution itself: whether it comes from God or from the devil, so that its outcome can be established more easily. For every matter is clearer once its author is known. It is enough, to be sure, to lay down as a preliminary rule that nothing happens without God's will. But we will not immediately give room to other debates on the basis of this statement, lest we be called away from the present point if someone should answer: "Then evil is from God, and wrongdoing is from God; nothing is left to the devil, nothing even to ourselves." The question now is about persecution. Concerning this, I will say for the moment that nothing happens without God's will, considering that persecution is above all worthy of God and, so to speak, necessary—namely for the testing of his servants or their rejection.

For what is the outcome of persecution, what other effect does it have, except the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord will certainly examine his own? Persecution is the Lord's judgment, through which each person is judged either tested or rejected. And judgment belongs to God alone. This is that winnowing fan which even now cleanses the Lord's threshing floor—that is, the church—scattering the confused heap of believers and separating the wheat of martyrs from the chaff of deniers. And this is also the ladder that Jacob dreamed of, showing some an ascent to higher things and others a descent to lower things (Genesis 28:12). So too persecution can be understood as a contest. By whom is the contest proclaimed, except by him by whom the crown and prizes are offered? You read the edict of this contest in Revelation, with what prizes it invites to victory—especially those who have properly conquered in persecution, struggling in victory not against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces of wickedness (Ephesians 6:12). So you will recognize that the decision of the contest belongs to the same contest-president who invites to the prize.

Everything that happens in persecution is for the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who raises up and casts down. And what belongs to the glory of God will certainly come about by his will. But when is God more believed, except when he is more feared—except in the time of persecution? The church is in astonishment. Then faith is more anxious in its expedition and more disciplined in fasts and vigils and prayers and humility, in mutual care and love, in holiness and sobriety. For there is no leisure except for fear and hope. And so from this very fact it is shown to us that what makes God's servants better cannot be attributed to the devil.

problems.quote: because something or other had been announced.
problems.why: Latin says the speaker does not know what was announced; English asserts an announcement was made, dropping the negation.
problems.fix: because I do not know what was being announced.
problems.ruling: "nescio quid" means 'I know not what'; English drops speaker's uncertainty, changing meaning.

edits.old: because something or other had been announced.
edits.new: because I do not know what was being announced.

fixed: Changed 'because something or other had been announced' to 'because I do not know what was being announced' to reflect the source's 'quod nescio quid annuntiaretur', which expresses uncertainty about what was announced.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening sentence so Fabius's question and Tertullian's uncertainty are distinct, smoothed sentence order and rhythm for reading aloud, and kept every claim, qualification, negation, quotation, and Scripture reference intact.
